extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political theory, comparative government, and constitutional design (scholars, policymakers, informed public)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the health and risks of democratic republics (especially the United States) with respect to majority power, institutional checks, public opinion, and the role of legal professionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of securities against tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: “Very inadequate securities which exist against tyranny.” When an individual or party is wronged in the United States, to whom can he apply for redress? (public opinion, legislature, executive, militia, jury, judges all controlled by the majority.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether institutional channels exist that allow redress independent of the majority's will. The text warns that if every instrument (opinion, legislature, executive, troops, jury, judges) is dominated by the majority, injured parties must simply submit. Example/anti-pattern: broad popular control of all instruments without safeguards leads to de facto despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation and independence of the three powers
rubrics_metrics.description: If the legislative power can represent the majority without being the slave of its passions; an executive retaining a degree of uncontrolled authority; and a judiciary independent of the other powers, a government could be democratic without risk of tyrannical abuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure whether legislature, executive, and judiciary have institutional independence and internal safeguards preventing capture by transient majorities. The page explicitly treats this configuration as a key security against majority tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection and enforcement of minority rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Majority may have made laws protecting minorities but, owing to prejudice and lack of magistrates' protection, minorities (e.g., freed blacks) are unable to exercise legal rights in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess not just the existence of minority-protecting laws but the ability and willingness of authorities to enforce them against majority hostility. Example: legal voting rights that are nullified by intimidation at the polls constitute a failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defined limits on public officers' authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The details of public office and the privileges which officers are to enjoy are rarely defined beforehand, enabling arbitrary authority; the majority treats officers as passive agents to be directed or reprimanded at every instant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether duties, powers, and tenure of officials are clearly specified to prevent arbitrary exercise of power. Lack of predefined limits is flagged as an enabler of administrative arbitrariness and habit-forming abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence from popular passions
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain States even the judges are elected by the majority; when the majority controls appointment or election of judges, judicial independence is undermined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate selection, tenure, and insulation mechanisms for judges. The author gives the acquittal of mob perpetrators and elected judges as evidence that majoritarian control can subvert justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of opinion and open discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: In America, when the majority has once irrevocably decided a question, all discussion ceases. Authors who step beyond the majority's accepted boundaries are tormented by obloquy and social persecution; freedom of opinion does not truly exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appraise whether public discourse remains open after majoritarian decisions and whether dissenters can speak without social or professional ruin. The presence of pervasive social censorship and self-censorship is a major deficiency according to the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral power of the majority (social coercion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority possesses a power which is physical and moral at the same time; it acts upon the will as well as upon the actions of men, repressing not only contest but controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for mechanisms of moral/social coercion (ostracism, professional exclusion, loss of patronage) that enforce conformity even without legal penalties. The text emphasizes this refined despotism as more dangerous because it enslaves thought while leaving bodies free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of the press and safeguards against mob violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Case of Baltimore (1812): a newspaper opposing the war had presses destroyed, editors attacked and one killed; militia failed to act; juries acquitted the guilty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the state's capacity and willingness to protect journalists and the press from extra-legal popular violence and to prosecute perpetrators. A healthy system enforces law against mobs and preserves a plural press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decentralized administration as a brake on central tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: The national majority must employ town and county magistrates to execute its decisions; local townships, municipal bodies, and counties act as concealed break-waters checking or parting the tide of popular excitement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the degree of administrative decentralization and local autonomy. Where central decrees rely on locally independent agents to execute, local structures can impede uniform administrative tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the legal profession as a conservative counterweight
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the legal profession derive habits of order, taste for formalities, and reverence for precedent that give them an aristocratic turn of mind and make them a powerful security against the excesses of democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the social and institutional influence of lawyers (bench and bar). The profession's orientation toward order, precedent, and legality is presented as a stabilizing element that can check majoritarian passions when integrated into government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent-based legal culture vs. reason-based advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The English and American lawyers have retained the law of precedents; they found opinions and decisions upon forefathers' decisions. 'The English and American lawyers investigate what has been done; the French advocate inquires what should have been done.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the legal culture privileges continuity (precedent) or abstract reasoning; a precedent-oriented system tends toward conservatism and legal stability, which the author views as protective against democratic excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between tyranny and arbitrary power
rubrics_metrics.description: Tyranny may be exercised by means of the law (and in that case it is not arbitrary); arbitrary power may be exercised for the good of the community (and then not tyrannical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this conceptual distinction to diagnose problems: identify whether abuses are legal but oppressive (tyranny via law) or arbitrary acts outside the law. Both are worrying but require different remedies (legal reform vs. administrative constraint).

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of centralized energetic government abusing force
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments of the American republics appear as much centralized and more energetic than absolute monarchies of Europe; democratic governments usually fail by abuse of force and misemployment of resources, not by impotence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess concentration of administrative energy and capacity; energetic centralization combined with weak restraints raises the risk of large-scale abuse. Historical warnings (Hamilton, Jefferson) are cited to underline this danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree to which public office invites currying favor and debases character
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic republics organized like the United States bring the practice of courting favor within the reach of the many; this extensive debasement of character checks the development of leading, independent persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the prevalence of patronage-seeking, dependence on popular favor, and social incentives that reward servility. Where 'currying favor' is widespread, the formation of independent, distinguished public figures is stunted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability that majority pressures will provoke minority resort to force (anarchy risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the unlimited authority of the majority urges the minorities to desperation, they may have recourse to physical force; anarchy will then be the result, but brought about by despotism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether persistent majoritarian oppression creates conditions likely to drive excluded groups toward extralegal resistance. The text frames one existential risk for republics as despotism-induced anarchy.
